title: Gecko found on a night hike in Nepal is one of 5 species scientists identified - Yahoo

full_article:
Unique creatures, odd animals and new species are discovered across the planet. This article is part of a collection of stories from McClatchy Media on recent species discoveries.

Deep-sea creature — waiting in 'glass sponges' to ambush — is new species in Pacific

The worm is iridescent and about 7 inches long, researchers said.

Off the southern coast of Japan, a new species of marine bristle worm, Eunice siphoninsidiator, was discovered living within the structure of glass sponges. These tube ambushing worms were found at depths of around 3,720 feet, showcasing iridescent bodies and dark brown mandibles. The discovery marks the first documented case of a eunicid inhabiting deep-sea sponges. | Read More

2-foot-long predator — with 'mesh pattern' on its eyes — discovered as new species

In the Yuanyang Guanyinshan Provincial Nature Reserve of southern China, researchers discovered a new species of pit viper named Ovophis zhaoermii. These "slender" vipers, with their distinctive mesh-patterned eyes, were found beside streams at night. The species is named in honor of the late Ermi Zhao, a renowned Chinese herpetologist. | Read More

'Long'-limbed creature with 'bent' toes found on walking trail. It's a new species

In central Nepal, scientists identified a new species called Cyrtodactylus chitwanensis, or the Chitwan bent-toed gecko, during their wildlife survey. A Cyrtodactylus karanshahi, or Karan’s bent-toed gecko.

In the Manaslu Conservation Area of northern Nepal, researchers discovered a new species of gecko named Cyrtodactylus karanshahi, or Karan's bent-toed gecko. This "medium-sized" gecko, with its "slender" body and "long" fingers, was found during a nighttime hike along a walking trail. The gecko's unique features and genetic divergence from related species led to its classification as a new species. | Read More

title: Nepal can host a 'Himalayan COP' in 2033 - Nepali Times
description: Nepal can host a 'Himalayan COP' in 2033  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
The 26 August climate-induced ice-rock avalanche in the Himalaya triggered a catastrophic debris flood along the Trisuli Corridor, killing thousands and destroying critical infrastructure. It shocked Nepal and stunned the world.

It also propelled Nepal to take the climate crisis and climate justice far more seriously, both domestically and internationally. Prime Minister Balendra Shah devoted his address to the UN General Assembly exclusively to climate justice.

Also at the UN, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal hosted the Sagarmatha to the Sea: A Call to Action for a Climate-Resilient Future, and highlighted climate justice at the ministerial meetings of the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the Group of 77 and China. He also raised the issue at the pre-COP 31 leaders’ event in Fiji and Tuvalu.

Finance Minister Swarnim Waglé is leading efforts to mobilise international solidarity and support for post-disaster recovery that is estimated to cost $5 billion.

Nepal is calling for international solidarity with all climate-vulnerable developing countries that contribute little to greenhouse gas emissions but suffer disproportionately from their effects. It is well placed to assume a leadership role on behalf of the world’s high-mountain regions, small islands, and coastal states.

Regrettably, despite mounting scientific evidence and disasters the current international climate is not conducive to action. Political leaders in many wealthy and powerful countries that have contributed substantially to global warming continue to deny the climate crisis or resist the measures needed to address it. Their support for long-term climate finance has been woefully inadequate.

Many wealthy and powerful countries are reducing overseas development assistance and increasing military spending. It is therefore difficult to expect a dramatic breakthrough in climate finance in the next few years.

The climate crisis, however, will not go away, it is likely to intensify and pose an existential threat to communities and countries around the world.

I recommend this 10-year strategy to strengthen Nepal’s leadership, build partnerships and establish Nepal as a serious and influential player in international climate negotiations.

1. Domestic Action

To be credible in its global advocacy, Nepal must demonstrate that it is doing everything within its capacity to respond to the climate crisis. Nepal already has an impressive community forestry program, promotion of electric vehicles, greater use of renewable energy and a range of mitigation and adaptation measures.

Its National Adaptation Plan for 2021–2050 and its Nationally Determined Contributions set out ambitious targets in agriculture, water resources, energy, forestry, biodiversity, and human health. Nepal is committed to achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2045.

Nepal should assemble a strong official delegation for the forthcoming COP31 and other fora, drawing on highly qualified experts not only from government but also academia and civil society. Members of the Nepali team should agree on a common set of national messages and speak with one voice in international forums.

Nepal should also strengthen domestic disaster-risk financing with more robust insurance schemes to protect private property and public assets, including hydroelectric plants. Urban, regional, and spatial development need reforms to counter rapid but poorly planned settlement growth and infrastructure development along snowed rivers. Some settlements will need to be relocated to safer areas, this could be costly and potentially controversial.

Nepal should aim to build a more disaster-resilient nation with holistic resettlement plans, ensuring access to jobs, schools, health care, transport, and other essential services.

2. Regional Action

As Prime Minister Shah observed in his UNGA address, rivers do not stop at borders, glaciers do not carry passports and floods do not need visas.

Nepal is advocating for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen joint early-warning systems, share scientific and satellite data, exchange technical expertise, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, and coordinate cross-border assistance. The mechanism could initially bring together China, India, and Nepal, then include all countries of the Hindu Kush Himalaya and High Mountain Asia. The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) could help convene and institutionalise such a mechanism.

3. Global Advocacy

Greenhouse gas emissions and wildfires affect sea levels, rainfall patterns, extreme weather, permafrost thaw and the melting of icecaps across the world. The crisis demands concerted global action guided by the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. Those that have historically contributed most to the problem and those with the greatest capacity to respond must do more.

Nepal should collaborate with leading universities specialising in climate science and policy, as well as research networks such as the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance to sharpen its negotiating positions.

Given uncertain prospects for substantial increases in the Loss and Damage Fund and other climate-finance mechanisms, including the Green Climate Fund and the Global Environment Facility, Nepal should work with least developed, landlocked and small island states to promote debt swaps for climate action.

4. Nepal in the COP Process

Nepal has had a prominent voice in recent climate summits, championing the Mountain Agenda and drawing attention to the effects of rapid glacier melt and extreme weather on Himalayan communities. It chaired the LDC negotiating group at COP18 in Doha and, in more recent COPs, has advocated for climate finance, Loss and Damage, direct access to climate funds, adaptation resources, and support for vulnerable, low-emitting mountain countries.

Nepal was particularly active at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, where it presented updated NDC targets, emphasised its commitment to carbon neutrality by 2045, and called for direct climate finance for mountain regions vulnerable to glacial melt and extreme weather. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, Nepal strongly supported operationalising the Loss and Damage Fund, highlighted climate-induced disasters in the Himalaya, and presented its $47 billion NAP roadmap.

Nepal is preparing to engage actively at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, next month. At a Pre-COP Leaders’ event in Fiji in October 2026, Nepal proposed a new international climate partnership linking the Himalaya with vulnerable Pacific Island states. The aim is to build a common front among mountain and ocean countries.

Nepal’s Minister of Agriculture, Forests and Environment, Gita Chaudhary, is attending the UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan before COP31. Armenia and Kyrgyzstan could therefore be natural partners with Nepal at COP31 and beyond in highlighting the particular needs of landlocked, mountainous developing countries.

Nepal should also seek a strong partnership with the Alliance of Small Island States, the main negotiating bloc representing 39 small island and low-lying coastal developing states. It should support AOSIS priorities at COP31, including pressing major greenhouse-gas emitters to accelerate emissions cuts to keep global warming to 1.5°C, securing rapid, direct-access funding through the Loss and Damage financing mechanism for vulnerable island communities, and accelerating the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy. In return, Nepal should seek explicit recognition of vulnerable mountain communities alongside island communities in relevant funding and policy priorities.

Nepal should mobilise its embassies in relevant countries to explain its priorities and advocate for them with governments and other influential stakeholders. Because Nepal does not have diplomatic missions in many small island states, its missions to the UN in New York and Geneva should take a lead in building partnerships with those countries.

5. Preparing for COP31 and Beyond

Nepal should advocate for a much better-resourced Loss and Damage Fund so that vulnerable countries can obtain more adequate support when future disasters strike, as they inevitably will.

Nepal should also propose a dedicated window for the rapid allocation and disbursement of funds when sudden, catastrophic events hit high-mountain countries. Such countries are particularly exposed to glacial outbursts and ice-rock avalanches that can cause extensive loss and damage downstream.

6. Hosting COP38 in 2033

The next possible opportunity for an Asia-Pacific country to host a climate summit would be COP33 in 2028. Several countries in the region have already expressed interest. A two-year preparation period would be unrealistic for Nepal. However, COP38 in 2033 would be a feasible and potentially transformative goal, allowing seven years to prepare before the Asia-Pacific region’s next expected turn.

The year 2033 would be especially meaningful because it marks the 80th anniversary of the first successful ascent of Mount Everest by Nepal’s Tenzing Norgay and New Zealand’s Edmund Hillary in 1953. Nepal could designate 2033 as ‘The Year of the Himalaya’ and present it as a ‘The Himalayan COP’. The outcome of COP38 could be framed as ‘The Himalayan Compact for Climate Justice’.

Nepal should announce its ambition and begin lobbying at COP31 in Antalya where a decision on the Asia-Pacific host for COP33 is likely to be made, and competition may be intense. Nepal could use its support for a COP33 host candidate as an opportunity to seek reciprocal support for Nepal’s COP38 bid. Beginning diplomatic outreach early would improve Nepal’s prospects and give it time to build support before any competing bids emerge.

The main reservation about selecting Nepal to host COP38 will likely be its current logistical and organisational capacity, including whether it can provide adequate facilities within the required timeframe. Nepal’s response should be to transform Kathmandu, Pokhara, Lumbini, and the Mount Everest region, into world-class international conference destinations in the next seven years.

The UNFCCC Secretariat’s formal COP preparation process typically takes about 18–24 months. It includes fact-finding and technical missions, followed by detailed planning for venues, transport, accommodation, security, and other arrangements. This process assumes that the host country already has - or can quickly develop - the necessary underlying capacity.

Once member states have reached agreement in principle on Nepal’s proposal to host COP38, Nepal should ask the UNFCCC Secretariat to begin its fact-finding and technical assessment well in advance. Rather than building a vast temporary ‘COP City’, Nepal should use COP38 as the target date for a seven-year national modernisation program demonstrating climate resilience and low-carbon design. The hosting arrangements themselves should become an example of enlightened climate action.

The country most vulnerable to Himalayan climate change would not merely be asking the world to talk about climate resilience. Nepal is demonstrating it.

7. A Road Map

2026–2027: Diplomatic groundwork to secure the right to host COP38

Establish a national COP38 task force

Consult Asia-Pacific countries and begin a diplomatic advocacy campaign

Develop a preliminary master plan for potential venues in Kathmandu, Pokhara, the Everest region, and possibly Lumbini

Engage the UNFCCC Secretariat on early fact-finding, technical missions, and venue assessments, and work toward a Host Country Agreement at the appropriate stage

2028–2029: Infrastructure planning

Select sites for conference facilities.

Expand convention capacity.

Ensure adequate hotel and other accommodation capacity.

Plan airport improvements.

Develop an integrated transport master plan.

Strengthen digital infrastructure.

Prepare comprehensive security plans.

2030–2031: Construction and implementation

Build or upgrade the main convention complex.

Develop temporary and permanent exhibition facilities.

Expand accommodation capacity.

Improve public transport, roads, and utilities.

Upgrade waste-management infrastructure.

Expand renewable-energy systems.

2032: Full-scale testing

Nepal should proactively host several major international events as dress rehearsals, including:

A Sagarmatha Sambaad

Climate-related preparatory conferences for mountain countries, LDCs, LLDCs, and other partners

Major Asia-Pacific conferences organised

Large tourism and convention events

2033: Everest 80 + COP38

By 2033 Nepal should have spent several years building an international coalition of mountain countries, LDCs, LLDCs, SIDS, and other climate-vulnerable developing countries facing Loss and Damage. Nepal would be better placed to present a coherent and compelling case for climate justice.

The Himalaya provide water and sustenance to nearly two billion people across more than a dozen Asian countries. Climate impacts therefore connect mountain systems to downstream populations and the world’s oceans. The coalition’s geographic narrative would be powerful and easy to communicate: Mountains → Rivers → Plains → Oceans.

Nepal’s climate diplomacy should have a multi-year legacy agenda rather than making COP38 a one-off event. The summit could become a milestone in Nepal’s journey toward climate resilience and recognition as a global leader championing climate justice for vulnerable countries.

8. Potential Constraints

Nepal will face significant challenges in realising this ambitious vision:

Sustaining political commitment

Maintaining continuity in leadership and management

Ensuring effective coordination

Securing adequate funding

Engaging young professionals, climate scientists, and civil society

If Nepal can summon the political will to address these challenges, it can aspire to lead a concerted national and global effort for climate justice. A carefully prepared bid to host COP38 in 2033 would turn Nepal’s acute climate vulnerability into a source of international leadership. The goal should be not simply to host a major conference, but to help secure lasting progress toward climate resilience and climate justice for Nepal and for vulnerable communities around the world.

title: We are Gandhians: Dipke Rejects Nepal, Bangladesh Protest Parallels - Deccan Chronicle
description: We are Gandhians: Dipke Rejects Nepal, Bangladesh Protest Parallels  Deccan Chronicle
publisher.title: Deccan Chronicle
full_article:
New Delhi: Amid escalating debate comparing youth protests in India to political unrest and regime changes in Nepal and Bangladesh, Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) activist Abhijeet Dipke on Tuesday issued a video statement on X.

Rejecting claims that local demonstrations mirror international turmoil, Dipke defended jailed activists Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, saying their calm compliance was proof of a purely Gandhian Satyagraha.

Addressing critics and commentators who cite global political volatility, ranging from violent youth riots in France to regime-change movements in Bangladesh and Nepal, Dipke urged observers to look at the adherence to non-violence displayed by Indian dissidents.

"To those constantly pointing fingers saying, 'Look at what is happening in France...' have some shame and look at what is happening right here in India. In India, Sourav Das and Ashutosh went to jail with smiles on their faces. They didn't do anything like what is happening elsewhere. Even when they knew they were being unlawfully imprisoned, they chose peace and compassion, entering prison with smiles rather than anger or hatred in their hearts," Dipke said.

Refusing to equate domestic civil dissent with violent overthrows, Dipke argued that the conduct of the imprisoned activists distinguishes Indian civil resistance from foreign movements.

"People talk about Nepal or Bangladesh, but look at our comrades: they went to jail smiling, without being provoked. They continue to embody Gandhian values—smiling on their way to jail, smiling inside the courtroom. You cannot instil hatred in them; hatred resides in you. And everyone can clearly see the state to which your hatred has brought this country," he added.

Dipke framed the activists' imprisonment not as a tool for chaotic overthrow, but as a moral awakening rooted in India’s historic independence struggle."

“Without wanting to draw direct comparisons, it reflects what Mahatma Gandhi did; when he was sent to jail, he went quietly because it was his Satyagraha. Ashutosh and Sourav are carrying out that exact same Satyagraha. By enduring that pain inside prison, they are awakening the conscience of this country. I cannot wait for them to be released," he stated.

Addressing state authorities and political opponents who view public gatherings as a threat to order, Dipke maintained that preventive detentions and prison terms would fail to break the morale of the movement or push it toward violence.

"If anyone thinks locking Sourav and Ashutosh up will intimidate or break them, that is never going to happen. I assure you, when they walk out, they will emerge with the same smiles, chanting 'Inquilab Zindabad' (Long Live the Revolution), continuing on Mahatma Gandhi's path of peace and non-violence—values we deeply believe in," Dipke added.

The judicial custody of Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka was extended by two days after their initial five-day judicial custody ended on Monday.

Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were taken back to judicial custody from Mandir Marg Police Station in Delhi after their surety was rejected over a reported mismatch in documents, their lawyers said.

Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) Court situated at Police Station Mandir Marg extended the custody till October 21.

title: The Dashain break is a chance to see more of Nepal and beyond - The Kathmandu Post
description: The Dashain break is a chance to see more of Nepal and beyond  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepalis living abroad are often asked the same question: “Have you been to Everest?” Some answer proudly. Others pause to think. Despite being home to the world’s highest mountain, Nepal remains a place many Nepalis have yet to explore fully.

For Archana KC Rana, senior manager at the Nepal Tourism Board’s Asia-Pacific desk, the question is a reminder that Nepalis should make time to see more of their own country. She believes everyone should visit the Everest region at least once in their lifetime.

“Wherever we go, people associate Nepal with Everest and assume we must have been there,” she says. “So we should see it for ourselves, find out what Everest looks like and where it stands.”

The long Dashain-Tihar holiday offers an opportunity to make that trip. Mid-September to mid-October mark Nepal’s autumn trekking season, when clear skies, mountain views and generally favourable weather draw walkers to the trails. Rather than spending the entire break visiting relatives, Rana suggests using a few days to explore the hills and mountains.

A trek in the Everest region can be more than a holiday for young Nepalis, she says. The journey through Lukla and Namche Bazar offers views of the world’s highest peak as well as an opportunity to learn about Sherpa culture and life in the Himalayas. But it is no easy walk, and travellers need to prepare properly.

Everest is not the only option. The Kanchenjunga region in eastern Nepal can also make for a rewarding autumn trek. For students in particular, Rana says, the journey offers a chance to learn about eastern Nepal’s landscape, tea gardens, local cultures and border regions.

The trip could also take in Sandakpur and Shree Antu. Mustang, with its starkly different geography, desert-like Himalayan landscapes, Thakali culture and distinctive architecture, is another of her recommendations. Such a journey can turn travel into a learning experience for children and young people, she says.

But enthusiasm alone is not enough when heading into the mountains. Rana urges people to check the weather before departure, stay in touch with local guides and tour operators, and keep family and friends informed throughout the journey.

Travellers need not head to high altitudes to experience Nepal’s culture. The Nepal Tourism Board also recommends lesser-known villages in the mid-hills, where visitors can experience local ways of life and the festive atmosphere without undertaking strenuous high-altitude treks.

For those drawn to wildlife and nature, Chitwan, Bardiya, Parsa, Shuklaphanta and Koshi Tappu offer alternatives. Temperatures in Chitwan and Bardiya become more comfortable in autumn, while Koshi Tappu is a popular destination for birdwatching.

Even those staying in the Kathmandu Valley do not have to travel far. The historic palace squares of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur are established attractions, but Rana suggests making time for older settlements and neighbourhoods such as Kirtipur, Bungamati, Khokana, Asan and Mangal Bazaar.

Her advice is to look beyond sightseeing and try to understand the places visited.

“The Kathmandu Valley itself is a living museum,” she says. “Spending an hour or two in a place, learning about its history and culture and talking to local people can make a trip much more rewarding.”

Dashain also marks the start of Nepal’s main trekking season. Mardi Himal, Annapurna Base Camp, Poon Hill, Ghorepani, Mustang, Tilicho Lake, the Annapurna Circuit, Manaslu and Everest Base Camp are among the most popular routes for Nepali travellers, according to Sagar Pandey, president of the Trekking Agencies’ Association of Nepal (TAAN).

But this year, he advises travellers to check the condition of roads and trails before setting off, as floods and landslides have affected some routes.

Altitude requires particular care. With roads now reaching Manang, travellers can gain elevation much faster than before, increasing the risk of altitude sickness if they do not allow their bodies enough time to adjust.

Post photo

“You should not go straight to a high altitude,” Pandey says. “Start from the lower elevations and trek upwards gradually, allowing your body to acclimatise.”

Driving to the mountains may save time, but beginning a trek at an elevation of 3,000 to 3,500 metres on the same day can be risky, he says.

Weather forecasts and official advisories should also be part of the preparation. “If I am going on a 10-day trip, I need to keep track of the weather and relevant government advisories throughout those 10 days,” Pandey says.

For trips that require a guide or trekking company, he recommends choosing an established operator. Travellers can check a company’s track record, services, reviews and TAAN membership before booking.

Beyond Nepal

For those planning to travel abroad, Southeast Asia remains a popular choice. Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Cambodia, along with Dubai, are among the preferred destinations for Nepali travellers, says Rajkumar Devkota, general secretary of the Nepal Association of Tour and Travel Agents (NATTA).

A four-night, five-day package to Vietnam costs around Rs165,000 to Rs170,000, he says. But travellers should consider visa requirements and costs before settling on a destination. “First, you need to check the visa fee and conditions. Then comes the cost of air tickets,” Devkota says. “You should also learn about the local culture.”

Rules and protocols vary by destination, making it important to research local requirements before travelling. Travel industry representatives say international airfares are at least 30 percent more expensive than last year. They advise travellers to compare ticket and package prices and book early.

International airlines have also introduced Dashain promotions to attract Nepali travellers. Qatar Airways has launched a Dashain-themed promotional offer in Nepal for the first time. Tickets can be purchased from October 7 to 22 for travel between October 10 and March 31 next year, the airline says. The offer applies to both economy and premium cabins, with discounts of up to 25 percent depending on the destination.

Sharik Bogati, Qatar Airways’ country manager for Nepal, says the promotion is intended to reflect Nepali culture while helping promote the country.

“We wanted to showcase Nepali culture and promote Nepal,” he says. “Dashain is a time when people start thinking about travel. Because the visa application process and other arrangements take time, we wanted people to use the festive period to plan their trips.”

The offer does not require passengers to travel during Dashain itself. Travellers can buy tickets during the promotional period and fly by March 31, the airline says. Nepalis living abroad, as well as foreign nationals and non-resident Nepalis planning to visit the country, can also purchase tickets.

Cathay Pacific offered discounts of 6 to 10 percent, depending on the destination, during the festival. The promotion covered Hong Kong, Australia, Japan, Canada, the United States, South Korea, China and the United Kingdom, says Juneu Maleku, the airline’s country manager for Nepal.

The Dashain-Tihar period is an important sales season for international airlines. Nepalis living abroad return home to celebrate with their families, while others travel overseas to visit relatives. This year’s extended holiday offers travellers plenty of choices, both within Nepal and beyond its borders.

For some, that could mean taking the trail towards Everest to see the world’s highest peak. For others, it could be an exploration of Mustang’s unusual landscape and culture. But wherever they go, the same rule applies: a longer holiday is no reason to rush into a trip.

Travellers should check their destination, weather conditions, road and trail access, visas, tickets, accommodation and local rules before setting out.

title: Nepali workers returning from India face overcharging at the border - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepali workers returning from India face overcharging at the border  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
For 52-year-old Kali Bahadur Sahakari, travelling to India for work has been a way of life for nearly four decades. He first went to Kalapahad in India’s Uttarakhand state at the age of 12 and still travels to the Garhwal and Almora regions for daily-wage work.

Much has changed over the years, he says, but two problems remain stubbornly familiar: harassment in the name of security checks at the border and being overcharged for transport.

Returning home for Dashain this year, Sahakari paid 250 Indian rupees to travel from Banbasa, a border town in India, to the Gaddachauki crossing in Nepal. The usual fare is around 50 rupees, with a small extra charge for luggage.

“This is never going to change. They always find some excuse to take more money,” he said. “The checks at every turn are never going to end either.”

Sahakari said checks on both sides of the border make the journey difficult. On the Indian side, workers carrying heavy loads have to queue for inspections and pass their belongings through X-ray machines, often waiting a long time with their luggage on their backs.

He still earns 500 to 600 rupees a day doing manual labour. Four decades ago, when his daily wage was just 10 to 20 rupees, he faced similar difficulties travelling to and from India. The wages have increased, but the problems along the route have barely changed, he said.

A resident of Pachaljharana Rural Municipality in Kalikot district, Sahakari heads to India each year after planting crops at home and returns in time for the harvest. This time, he came back from Almora to celebrate Dashain with his family.

His work in Almora includes breaking stones and carrying soil and bricks. His earnings must cover his own food and accommodation as well as his family’s expenses back home.

“The cost of travel and almost everything else has gone up, but our wages have increased very little,” he said. “It is difficult to cover our living expenses and support our families on what we earn.”

He plans to return to India after Tihar, once he has brought in the harvest and sown wheat.

Bishal BK, another migrant worker from Kalikot, said the extra transport charges eat into the savings workers set aside for festivals.

“Whenever we return home, we are charged more. Sometimes they blame it on our luggage; other times, they say it is for the checks,” he said. “The money we save from manual labour for the festivals gets spent on the journey itself.”

BK paid 200 rupees for the trip from Banbasa to Gaddachauki this time, even though the fare with luggage would normally be around 100 rupees.

The overcharging does not stop at the border. In Nepal, the usual fare from Gaddachauki to Mahendranagar is 50 Nepali rupees, but returning workers are now often charged 100 rupees, with luggage cited as the reason.

Despite the extra costs, workers rarely file complaints. Eager to get home and doubtful that they will receive timely redress, many simply pay and continue their journey.

title: Nepal Premier League to introduce DRS for third edition - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal Premier League to introduce DRS for third edition  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The Nepal Premier League will introduce the Decision Review System (DRS) in its third edition, scheduled to run from October 26 to November 21.

The Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) announced the move on social media on Tuesday, paving the way for teams to challenge on-field umpiring decisions during the tournament.

CAN Secretary Paras Khadka had earlier said preparations were underway to bring DRS to the league. According to Khadka, two companies had already tested the technology, with a final decision to be made after assessing its accuracy and reliability.

CAN said the system would use full 3D ball-tracking technology to review leg-before-wicket (LBW) decisions. Reviews would also be available for run-outs, stumpings and no-ball calls.

The system will also use artificial intelligence-based edge detection to determine whether the ball has touched the bat, helping umpires assess potential edges.

title: Ayushmann Khurrana, Sara Ali Khan's Udta Teer Banned In Nepal Ahead Of October 23 Release? - iDiva
description: Ayushmann Khurrana, Sara Ali Khan's Udta Teer Banned In Nepal Ahead Of October 23 Release?  iDiva
publisher.title: iDiva
full_article:
Ayushmann Khurrana and Sara Ali Khan’s upcoming film Udta Teer seems to have already hit a roadblock ahead of its release on October 23. Reports suggest that Nepal has denied permission for the film’s public screening — a decision that comes after Nepal’s Central Film Censor Board reviewed the movie and found that it violates a provision of the country’s cinema law.

However, the exact reason for banning the movie hasn’t been publicly announced yet.

Udta Teer banned in Nepal?

According to a report by India Today , Nepal’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology has informed the film’s local distributor, National Cine Group Nepal Pvt. Ltd., through an official letter. As of now, the film’s public exhibition has not received permission from the censor board.

Reports suggest that the decision is based on a provision of the National Cinema (Production, Exhibition and Distribution) Act. The Central Film Censor Board has come to a conclusion after review that the film’s production fell under content that is prohibited by the legislation.

While the explicit details haven’t been revealed, Udta Teer tells the story of an India-Pakistan espionage mission, and it could face similar objections . The movie follows a Pakistani spy who makes his way into India, but then loses his memory when he is met with an accident, and eventually believes that he is an Indian counterterrorism officer.

Since the movie is now banned, it is also restricted from screening in Nepal.

Along with Ayushmann Khurrana and Sara Ali Khan, the movie also features Mukul Dev, Ram Kapoor, Raghubir Yadav, Brijendra Kala, Gulshan Grover, Suhail Nayyar, Rahul Bose and Supriya Pilgaonkar. Written and directed by Akash A. Kaushik, Udta Teer is scheduled to release in cinemas on October 23, 2026.

title: Alpine Style in Nepal: A New Route While Others Retreat - Explorersweb »
description: Alpine Style in Nepal: A New Route While Others Retreat  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
Several small teams are attempting difficult climbs on Nepal’s 6,000’ers and 7,000’ers. Unfortunately, they rarely report on their plans or progress until they return, and often only if they succeed.

This is what we know about the ongoing expeditions.

Peak 41

A team of young French climbers, members of the Military High Mountain Group (GMHM) from Chamonix, celebrated the 50th anniversary of the GMHM with a new route on Peak 41. This 6,654m mountain is located in the Khumbu region and is often called the “true Mera Peak.”

Team members Konrad Piontek, Amaury Fouillade, and Clovis Paulin took advantage of a good weather window and achieved the first ascent of the peak’s northeast face. They climbed in an alpine-style single push over four days. The result is a beautiful 1,400m line with difficulties up to ED+ 5+ M6 A1 90°. They descended via the southeast face. The team named their line Bon Matin (good morning).

Jugal II

Nivel Meroi and Romano Benet are acclimatized and ready to attempt a new route on Jugal II, but the Italian couple will be on their own. Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, has left due to illness.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Jannu

Meanwhile, in the Kangchenjunga region, a large Russian team has also finished acclimatizing. The team has trekked in the area and crossed a number of high-altitude passes, the latest of them at the top of an icefall at 5,750m. They reported lots of snow above 5,000mbut are ready to attempt a new route on the formidable Jannu (7,710m) from its southeast side.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

The team comprises Ivan Artemov, Ivan Volkov, Artem Zhdanov, Konstantin Neumoin, Roman Shilin, and Vasily Yagodin.

Gangapurna West

Hidesuke Taneishi and Tetsu Hashimoto of Japan travelled to Nepal in September, aiming to achieve the first ascent of Gangapurna West (7,455m), also known as Asapurna or Peak Lachenal. They have provided no news since, but they probably had to retreat when an intense snowstorm hit the Annapurna region three weeks ago.

Location of Gangapurna West on a Google Earth screenshot. Notes by Linday Griffin for the American Alpine Journal.

Meanwhile, a second team has reached the base of the peak with the same objective. Valery Shamalo, Natalia Zanina, Maksim Trufanov, and Ruslan Kirichenko reached the mountain at the beginning of October and saw no one else there. They reported that recent precipitation had left the trail in a poor state; the climbers had to cross landslides and swollen rivers to reach Base Camp.

A member of the Russian team heading for Gangapurna West/Asapurna. Photo: Natalia Zanina

The team has completed two acclimatization climbs, looking for a passage through the icefall at the base of the mountain and then a series of couloirs. They reached 5,900m and, on a second trip, 6,600m. Deep snow covered the peak, which slowed progress. Finally, they launched a summit bid last week.

From 6,600m, they spent a day on technical ice sections that were 70–80º steep. In poor visibility, they endured spindrift and were showered by small ice chunks. “In the afternoon, the weather deteriorated sharply. Heavy snowfall began, and we started being struck by large, continuous avalanches. At 6,800m (340m from the summit), we decided to turn back,” Natalia Zanina said.

https://explorersweb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/video-gangapurna.mp4

A note on names: according to 8000ers.com , Asapurna should be the correct name for this peak because — although it is closer to Gangapurna — Asapurna’s summit ridge connects directly to Annapurna III.

Mystery teams

The list of climbing permits granted by Nepal’s Ministry of Tourism points to some other interesting expeditions, some of them in remote western Nepal. There is a permit for Nyalu Kang (6,265m), only opened to foreign climbers in 2024 and reportedly unclimbed, and Ardang, summited once, by Canadians Bryce Kendall and Sunny Twelker in 2019. Victor Saunders and Mick Fowler of the UK attempted Ardang last year.
